prompt: A semiconductor was run with ISMEAR = 0 and SIGMA = 0.05. Which energy should you use for energy differences?

options.text: energy(sigma->0), printed as E0 in OSZICAR
options.why: With Gaussian smearing the energy and the free energy err by equal and opposite amounts of order sigma squared, so their average, energy(sigma->0), removes the leading smearing error.

options.text: free energy TOTEN
options.why: Tempting, because the forces belong to it, but it still carries the -T*S term; for Gaussian smearing the sigma->0 value is the better estimate of the zero-smearing energy.

options.text: energy without entropy
options.why: It has the same size of smearing error as TOTEN with the opposite sign; only the average of the two cancels it.

options.text: The energy of the first electronic step
options.why: The first electronic step is far from self-consistency; only the converged energy of the last step means anything.

hints: Smearing adds an entropy term. Which printed energy tries to remove its effect?
Which scheme is this run using, and for which scheme is the average of E and F derived?

visual.caption: Gaussian occupation against energy, in units of the width.
visual.alt: Curve of the Gaussian occupation falling smoothly from 1 to 0 across the Fermi level.

prompt: Why are DFT total energies only meaningful as differences between runs with matched settings?

options.text: The energy zero depends on the POTCARs, ENCUT and functional, and only cancels when these match
options.why: Each potential and basis sets its own reference energy; with identical settings the offsets are the same in both runs and drop out of the difference.

options.text: VASP adds a random constant to every run
options.why: The offset is not random: the same input gives the same energy. It is a systematic offset set by the potentials and the basis.

options.text: Total energies are never converged
options.why: Convergence matters, but even a fully converged total energy depends on the potentials used; the difference is what is physical.

options.text: VASP reports energies in arbitrary units
options.why: The energies are in eV; the issue is the reference point, not the unit.

hints: What happens to the total energy if you swap Ti for Ti_pv?
Which part of the energy is the same in two runs with identical settings?

visual.caption: A series of runs that will be compared.
visual.alt: A three-step flow from fixing one settings block, to running each structure, to comparing the energies.

prompt: A 32-atom metal cell has EENTRO = -0.064 eV in OUTCAR. What is the absolute value of T*S per atom, in meV per atom?
hints: Divide the absolute value of EENTRO by the number of atoms.
0.002 eV is how many meV? Compare the result with the 1 meV per atom rule of thumb.

visual.caption: Methfessel-Paxton occupation for one smearing width.
visual.alt: Curve of the occupation against energy from the Fermi level in eV, falling from 1 to 0 with a small dip and overshoot.

prompt: The last TOTAL-FORCE block of a relaxation shows a largest force of 0.035 eV/Angstrom, and the INCAR has EDIFFG = -0.02. What does this tell you?

options.text: The relaxation has not met its force criterion yet
options.why: A negative EDIFFG asks for every force to be below 0.02 eV/Angstrom; 0.035 is above it, so the run would continue, or stopped at NSW.

options.text: It is converged, because 0.035 is smaller than 1
options.why: The criterion is the absolute value of EDIFFG in eV/Angstrom, not 1; the force must be below 0.02.

options.text: It is converged, because a negative EDIFFG compares energies
options.why: It is the other way round: a negative EDIFFG is the force criterion, a positive one compares energies.

options.text: The units do not match, so nothing can be said
options.why: Both the forces in OUTCAR and a negative EDIFFG are in eV per angstrom, so they compare directly.

hints: What does the sign of EDIFFG decide?
Compare the largest force with the absolute value of EDIFFG.

visual.caption: Largest force at each ionic step of a relaxation (illustrative).
visual.alt: Falling curve of the largest force against ionic step on a logarithmic axis, with a dashed tolerance line.

prompt: A metal is relaxed with ISMEAR = 1 (Methfessel-Paxton) and SIGMA = 0.1. Which energy is the safer one to report, and what should you check?

options.text: TOTEN, the free energy, after checking that T*S per atom is small
options.why: The (E + F)/2 average is derived for Gaussian smearing, where the errors are equal and opposite. Methfessel-Paxton removes the leading error differently, so use F at a small width and check the entropy term.

options.text: energy(sigma->0), because the average is exact for every scheme
options.why: Tempting, since VASP prints it for every run, but the average rests on the Gaussian error pattern and has no such justification for Methfessel-Paxton.

options.text: energy without entropy, because it has no smearing in it
options.why: It still comes from smeared occupations; dropping the -T*S term does not remove the smearing error.

options.text: Any of them, because smearing never changes the energy
options.why: Smearing does change the energy, by an amount that grows with SIGMA; that is why the entropy term is checked.

hints: For which smearing scheme is the sigma->0 average derived?
Which printed energy belongs to the forces?

visual.caption: Occupation for two smearing schemes, in units of the width.
visual.alt: Two occupation curves against energy in units of the width: a smooth Gaussian one and a Methfessel-Paxton one with a small dip and overshoot.

prompt: A cell of compound AB2 holds 2 formula units (6 atoms) and has E = -42.00 eV. The element references give -5.20 eV per A atom and -6.40 eV per B atom. What is the formation energy in eV per atom? (Illustrative numbers.)
hints: Subtract 2 A atoms and 4 B atoms at their reference energies from the cell energy.
Divide what is left by the 6 atoms in the cell.

items.label: Divide by the number of atoms

visual.caption: Building a formation energy from three runs.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: take the cell energy, subtract the element reference energies, divide by the number of atoms.

prompt: What does a negative EDIFFG, for example EDIFFG = -0.02, tell VASP to check?

options.text: That the force on every atom is below 0.02 eV/Angstrom
options.why: A negative value switches EDIFFG to a force criterion: the run stops when the largest force magnitude falls below its absolute value.

options.text: That the energy change between ionic steps is below 0.02 eV
options.why: That is what a positive EDIFFG does; it can stop while forces are still large.

options.text: That the pressure is below 0.02 kB
options.why: The force criterion ignores the stress; in cell relaxations you check the stress separately.

options.text: That the electronic loop converged to 0.02 eV
options.why: The electronic loop is controlled by EDIFF, not EDIFFG.

hints: The sign of EDIFFG picks between two kinds of criterion.
Which quantity is in eV per angstrom?

visual.alt: Falling curve of the largest force against ionic step on a logarithmic axis, with a dashed tolerance line.

prompt: An ISIF = 3 relaxation of a bulk crystal finished, but a second run from its CONTCAR changes the volume again. What is the best next step?

options.text: Raise ENCUT to about 1.3 times the largest ENMAX and repeat from CONTCAR until the volume stops changing
options.why: VASP keeps the plane-wave basis of the starting cell, so the stress carries a Pulay error. A higher cutoff shrinks it and each restart builds a basis for the new cell.

options.text: Accept the first result, since the first run reached required accuracy
options.why: Reaching the force criterion does not remove the Pulay stress; the volume can still be biased.

options.text: Lower ENCUT so the run is faster and repeat
options.why: A lower cutoff makes the Pulay stress larger, not smaller.

options.text: Switch to ISIF = 2 and report that volume
options.why: ISIF = 2 freezes the cell at whatever volume it has, which does not fix the bias.

hints: Why might the stress of a cell relaxation be biased?
What does a restart from CONTCAR rebuild?

prompt: Which line in OUTCAR confirms that the ionic relaxation met its EDIFFG criterion?

options.text: reached required accuracy
options.why: VASP prints this when the ionic stopping criterion set by EDIFFG is met, before it stops.

options.text: General timing and accounting informations for this job
options.why: This shows the run ended normally, which also happens when it stops at NSW without converging.

options.text: aborting loop because EDIFF is reached
options.why: That marks the end of one electronic loop, not of the ionic relaxation.

options.text: The last F= line of OSZICAR
options.why: OSZICAR prints one F= line per ionic step whether or not the relaxation has converged.

hints: Which loop does EDIFFG control, and which EDIFF?
A normal end of a job is not the same as a converged one.

prompt: Which file holds the latest structure of a relaxation, in a form you can copy straight to POSCAR to restart?

options.text: CONTCAR
options.why: CONTCAR is rewritten after every ionic step in POSCAR format, so it holds the latest geometry even if the job stops early.

options.text: POSCAR
options.why: POSCAR is the input; VASP never updates it.

options.text: XDATCAR
options.why: XDATCAR holds the whole trajectory; its last frame has the same positions, but it is not a POSCAR-format restart file.

options.text: OUTCAR
options.why: OUTCAR prints positions in its force tables, but not in a format VASP reads as a structure.

hints: Which file has the same format as POSCAR?
Which file is updated after every ionic step?

visual.alt: Four input files feeding VASP and five output files coming out.

prompt: You start a relaxation from a rough structure with large forces. Which IBRION is the robust first choice?

options.text: IBRION = 2, conjugate gradient
options.why: Conjugate gradient with line minimizations is the robust standard for rough starts; RMM-DIIS can take over close to the minimum.

options.text: IBRION = 1, RMM-DIIS quasi-Newton
options.why: It is efficient near the minimum, but with large forces far from it it can be unstable.

options.text: IBRION = 0
options.why: That is molecular dynamics, not a relaxation.

options.text: IBRION = -1
options.why: That is a static run: the ions do not move at all.

hints: Which optimizer is described as robust far from the minimum?
Two of the options do not relax the structure at all.

visual.caption: The allowed number of ionic steps in a relaxation.
visual.alt: A row of boxes for ionic steps, with a note that up to 100 steps are allowed.

prompt: You relax a metal surface slab with 15 angstrom of vacuum. Which ISIF should you use?

options.text: ISIF = 2: ions move, the cell stays fixed
options.why: The vacuum and the in-plane cell are set on purpose; relaxing the ions only keeps them.

options.text: ISIF = 3: ions, shape and volume
options.why: Vacuum has no stress to resist, so the cell would shrink into it.

options.text: ISIF = 7: volume only
options.why: The atoms would not relax, and the vacuum would still be free to change.

options.text: ISIF = 4: ions and cell shape at fixed volume
options.why: The volume stays fixed, but the cell shape may still shear and stretch, which distorts the vacuum and the in-plane lattice.

hints: What would happen to the vacuum if the cell could change?
Which ISIF moves ions only and keeps the cell?

visual.caption: The (111) plane of an fcc crystal, a common surface for slabs.
visual.alt: Face-centred cubic cell with the (111) plane drawn as a triangle through three cube corners.

prompt: Before you read a DOS plot from a non-self-consistent (ICHARG = 11) DOS run, how should you shift the energy axis?

options.text: Subtract E-fermi taken from the OUTCAR of the self-consistent run
options.why: DOSCAR energies are absolute, and the Fermi level written by an ICHARG = 11 run can be shifted; the SCF value is the reliable one.

options.text: Subtract the E-fermi written by the ICHARG = 11 run
options.why: Tempting, since it is in the same folder, but a Fermi level from a non-self-consistent run can be shifted.

options.text: No shift is needed; DOSCAR energies are already relative to E_F
options.why: They are absolute; line 6 gives E_F so that you can subtract it.

options.text: Shift so that the lowest state sits at zero
options.why: The convention is E - E_F = 0 (or the VBM for semiconductors), so that filled and empty states are read off at a glance.

hints: Are DOSCAR energies absolute or relative?
Which run determined the occupations self-consistently?

visual.alt: A histogram of how many levels fall at each energy, drawn sideways along the energy axis.

prompt: A DOS made with ISMEAR = 0 and SIGMA = 0.1 shows a smaller gap than the band structure. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Gaussian broadening puts tails of width a few SIGMA into the gap
options.why: Each level is drawn as a Gaussian bell of width SIGMA; its tails reach into the gap from both edges, so the gap looks narrower than the eigenvalues say.

options.text: The DOS run used a different functional
options.why: Possible in principle, but nothing in the setup suggests it; broadening alone explains a smaller apparent gap.

options.text: The band structure always overestimates gaps
options.why: Bands and DOS come from the same eigenvalues; the band plot shows them without broadening.

options.text: NEDOS was too large
options.why: A finer energy grid resolves the edges better; it does not shrink the gap.

hints: What does SIGMA do to each level in the DOS?
Which plot shows the eigenvalues without any broadening?

visual.caption: The broadened delta function of Gaussian smearing.
visual.alt: A bell-shaped curve centred on zero, the energy axis in units of the smearing width.

prompt: Which LORBIT value is the usual choice for site- and lm-resolved PDOS (s, py, pz, px, dxy, ...) in DOSCAR?

options.text: LORBIT = 11
options.why: 11 resolves each atom's projection into the individual p and d orbitals and takes the sphere radii from the POTCAR.

options.text: LORBIT = 10
options.why: 10 gives s, p and d per atom, but not the individual m components.

options.text: LORBIT = 12
options.why: 12 has the same projections as 11 and adds phase factors to PROCAR, which a PDOS does not need.

options.text: NEDOS = 3001
options.why: NEDOS sets the energy grid, not the projections.

hints: Which value splits p into px, py and pz?
Which value adds phase information you rarely need?

visual.caption: A slice through one p orbital.
visual.alt: A two-lobed p orbital shape drawn in the xz plane, one lobe positive and one negative.

prompt: You want a sharp, accurate total DOS of a bulk semiconductor on a dense uniform Gamma-centred mesh. Which ISMEAR fits?

options.text: ISMEAR = -5, the tetrahedron method with Blochl corrections
options.why: It interpolates the bands between k-points and gives sharp edges and accurate DOS for bulk cells on a uniform mesh with at least 4 k-points.

options.text: ISMEAR = 1 with SIGMA = 0.2
options.why: Methfessel-Paxton is for metals and gives wrong energies and occupations for semiconductors.

options.text: ISMEAR = 0 with SIGMA = 0.5
options.why: A width this large blurs the peaks and fills the gap with tails.

options.text: ISMEAR = -5 on a line-mode path
options.why: The tetrahedron method needs a uniform mesh that fills the zone; a path does not.

hints: Which method uses the mesh geometry itself instead of a broadening width?
Which scheme should never be used on semiconductors?

visual.caption: An 8 by 8 Gamma-centred k-point mesh (2D slice).
visual.alt: A square grid of 8 by 8 k-points with one point at the zone centre.

prompt: A DOS run uses EMIN = -10, EMAX = 15 and NEDOS = 2501. What is the spacing of the energy grid, in eV?
hints: The window is EMAX minus EMIN.
There are NEDOS - 1 intervals between NEDOS points.

visual.caption: Working out the energy resolution of a DOS run.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: find the window width, find the number of intervals, divide one by the other.

prompt: In a spin-polarized DOSCAR, the integrated DOS at the Fermi level is 14.6 electrons for spin up and 12.4 for spin down. What is the total magnetic moment of the cell, in Bohr magnetons?
hints: The moment is the number of up electrons minus the number of down electrons.
Each unpaired electron contributes one Bohr magneton.

prompt: On a transition-metal surface, the d-band center moves closer to the Fermi level. In the Hammer-Norskov model, what does that usually mean?

options.text: Adsorbates bind more strongly
options.why: A higher d-band center leaves the antibonding adsorbate-metal states emptier, so binding gets stronger; the d-band center tracks this trend.

options.text: Adsorbates bind more weakly
options.why: That is the trend for a center moving down, away from the Fermi level.

options.text: The surface becomes an insulator
options.why: The d-band center is a first moment of the d PDOS; it says nothing by itself about a gap opening.

options.text: Nothing, because the d-band center depends only on SIGMA
options.why: Broadening changes the shape of the PDOS a little, but the center is set by the electronic structure; compare centers at matched settings.

hints: The d-band center is the average energy of the d states.
Closer to E_F means the antibonding states with an adsorbate are pushed up and emptied.

visual.caption: Number of levels at each energy in a toy material. Toy model.
visual.alt: A histogram of how many levels fall at each energy, drawn sideways along the energy axis.

prompt: When is a band gap called indirect?

options.text: When the valence-band maximum and the conduction-band minimum sit at different k-points
options.why: An indirect gap needs a change of crystal momentum to cross, which a photon alone cannot supply, as in silicon.

options.text: When the gap is smaller than 1 eV
options.why: The size of the gap does not decide whether it is direct or indirect.

options.text: When the valence-band maximum and the conduction-band minimum sit at the same k-point
options.why: That is the definition of a direct gap, as in GaAs.

options.text: When spin-orbit coupling is switched on
options.why: Spin-orbit coupling can change the band edges, but the definition is about where in k they sit.

hints: Look at the k-point of the top of the filled bands and of the bottom of the empty bands.
Light carries almost no crystal momentum.

visual.caption: Real and reciprocal lattice vectors of the fcc lattice.
visual.alt: Primitive fcc cell with its three real-space lattice vectors and the three reciprocal vectors.

prompt: Why should you not use ISMEAR = -5 in a band-structure run on a line-mode path?

options.text: The tetrahedron method needs a uniform mesh that tiles the whole Brillouin zone, and a path does not
options.why: Tetrahedra are built between neighbouring points of a 3D mesh; points along lines cannot form them.

options.text: Because ISMEAR = -5 is only for metals
options.why: It is used for insulators and metals alike on a uniform mesh; the problem here is the path.

options.text: Because it makes the bands smoother than they are
options.why: The occupations scheme does not change the eigenvalues on the path; the method simply cannot be built on a line.

options.text: Because the path has too many k-points
options.why: The number is not the issue: even a dense path does not fill the zone.

hints: What geometric objects does the tetrahedron method need?
Do points along a few lines fill a volume?

visual.caption: Real and reciprocal lattice vectors of the fcc lattice.
visual.alt: Primitive fcc cell with its three real-space lattice vectors and the three reciprocal vectors.

prompt: What does KPOINTS_OPT (VASP 6.3 and newer) change in the band-structure workflow?

options.text: The path is evaluated in the same job, after the SCF converges on the uniform mesh in KPOINTS
options.why: VASP converges the density on the uniform mesh and then computes the eigenvalues on the KPOINTS_OPT path, so no separate ICHARG = 11 run is needed.

options.text: It makes PBE band gaps agree with experiment
options.why: It changes how the path is computed, not the functional; PBE still underestimates gaps.

options.text: It lets the SCF run on the path alone, without a uniform mesh
options.why: The density still needs the uniform mesh; a path cannot converge it.

options.text: It works in VASP 5.4 as well
options.why: It is a VASP 6.3 feature; older versions use the two-step ICHARG = 11 route.

hints: Which file still holds the uniform mesh?
How many runs does the classic route need?

visual.alt: Three stages in a row, relaxation then SCF in the same folder then a band or density-of-states run, with the file that travels along each arrow.

prompt: In the two-step ICHARG = 11 band workflow, which settings must be identical to the SCF run that wrote CHGCAR? Select all that apply.

options.text: ENCUT
options.why: The fixed density belongs to one basis; a different cutoff no longer matches it.

options.text: ISPIN and MAGMOM
options.why: A spin-polarized density read into a non-spin run, or with other moments, gives a different Hamiltonian.

options.text: LMAXMIX for d or f elements
options.why: It sets how much of the one-centre density CHGCAR keeps; a mismatch loses d or f occupation information.

options.text: NBANDS
options.why: You may raise NBANDS in the band run to see more conduction bands; the density is frozen, so this is safe.

options.text: The KPOINTS file
options.why: This is the one thing that must change: the band run uses the path instead of the uniform mesh.

hints: Which settings define the Hamiltonian that the frozen density belongs to?
Which two things are you meant to change in the band run?

visual.alt: Three stages in a row, relaxation then SCF in the same folder then a band or density-of-states run, with the file that travels along each arrow.

prompt: Near a conduction-band minimum, a fit gives d2E/dk2 = 38.1 eV Angstrom^2 (k in Cartesian inverse angstrom, 2 pi included). Using hbar^2/m_e = 7.62 eV Angstrom^2, what is m*/m_e? (Illustrative numbers.)
hints: m*/m_e = (hbar^2/m_e) divided by the curvature.
7.62 divided by 38.1.

prompt: Your band plot stops just above the conduction-band minimum: the higher conduction bands are missing. What is the fix?

options.text: Raise NBANDS in the ICHARG = 11 band run
options.why: VASP computes only NBANDS bands, and the default adds few empty ones. With the density frozen, more bands cost a little time and change nothing else.

options.text: Raise ENCUT
options.why: The cutoff sets the basis quality, not how many bands are computed.

options.text: Rerun the SCF with a denser k-mesh
options.why: A denser SCF mesh changes the density sampling, not the number of bands on the path.

options.text: Switch to ISMEAR = -5
options.why: The tetrahedron method cannot be used on a path, and smearing does not add bands.

hints: Which tag sets how many bands VASP computes?
Is it safe to change it when the density is frozen?

prompt: How do you turn a raw CHGCAR grid value into an electron density in e per cubic angstrom?

options.text: Divide it by the cell volume in cubic angstrom
options.why: CHGCAR stores rho times the cell volume, so dividing by V gives rho itself.

options.text: Multiply it by the cell volume
options.why: The volume is already multiplied in; multiplying again makes it worse.

options.text: Divide it by the number of grid points
options.why: Dividing the sum of all values by the number of points gives the electron count, not the density at one point.

options.text: Use it as it is
options.why: The values are scaled by the volume, so they are too large by V.

hints: What is stored: rho, or rho times something?
Averaging all grid values gives the number of electrons.

visual.alt: A single hump of electron density across a box, highest in the middle and zero at the walls.

prompt: In which order does VASP write the 3D grid values in CHGCAR?

options.text: x fastest, then y, then z
options.why: This is Fortran order: the index is ix + nx * (iy + ny * iz).

options.text: z fastest, then y, then x
options.why: That is C order; reading CHGCAR this way distorts non-cubic cells and moves the density off the atoms.

options.text: In random order, with coordinates on every line
options.why: No coordinates are written; the position of each value follows from its place in the list.

options.text: Atom by atom, around each nucleus
options.why: The values are on a regular grid over the whole cell, not grouped by atoms.

hints: Is VASP written in Fortran or C?
What changes fastest when you read the numbers in order?

visual.alt: Four input files feeding VASP and five output files coming out, with CHGCAR emphasised.

prompt: What does the second data block of a spin-polarized (ISPIN = 2) CHGCAR hold?

options.text: The magnetization density, rho up minus rho down, times the cell volume
options.why: The first block is the total density, the second the spin difference; together they give both channels.

options.text: The spin-down density alone
options.why: Tempting, but VASP stores the difference; spin down is (total minus magnetization) divided by 2.

options.text: The electrostatic potential
options.why: The potential is written to LOCPOT, not CHGCAR.

options.text: The density of the second SCF iteration
options.why: CHGCAR holds only the density of the last electronic step.

hints: The two blocks let you rebuild both spin channels.
Which combination is zero in a non-magnetic material?

visual.alt: Eight atoms in a 2 by 2 by 2 cubic cell, every moment pointing up.

prompt: How does LOCPOT differ from CHGCAR in scaling?

options.text: LOCPOT holds a potential in eV that is not multiplied by the cell volume
options.why: It uses the same grid layout, but the values are the potential itself, so you plot or average them directly.

options.text: LOCPOT is also multiplied by the volume, like CHGCAR
options.why: Only the density files carry the volume factor; dividing LOCPOT by V would give nonsense.

options.text: LOCPOT is written on a coarser grid with a different axis order
options.why: It uses the same grid layout and axis order as CHGCAR.

options.text: LOCPOT stores the density in e per cubic angstrom
options.why: LOCPOT is a potential, not a density.

hints: Which quantity does LOCPOT hold?
Does a potential need a volume factor?

visual.alt: Four input files feeding VASP and five output files coming out, with CHGCAR emphasised.

prompt: You want the charge density difference for a molecule adsorbed on a slab (AB = molecule on slab). How should the runs for A and B be done?

options.text: Static runs of each part at its position in the relaxed AB, in the same cell and on the same FFT grid
options.why: Then the only difference between the three densities is the interaction; the grid points line up one to one for the subtraction.

options.text: Relax the molecule and the slab separately first
options.why: The difference would then mix the bonding with the change of geometry.

options.text: Put the molecule in a smaller box to save time
options.why: A different cell gives a different grid, and the points no longer line up.

options.text: Let each run choose its own default FFT grid
options.why: Defaults can differ between runs; copy NGXF, NGYF and NGZF so that every grid is the same.

hints: What must line up point by point for a subtraction to mean anything?
Should the parts be allowed to change shape?

prompt: In an ELF map of a crystal, a large region has ELF close to 0.5. What does that suggest?

options.text: The electrons there behave like a uniform electron gas, as in a metal
options.why: ELF is built so that a uniform electron gas gives exactly 0.5; metallic regions sit near this value.

options.text: Half an electron sits in that region
options.why: ELF is a localization measure between 0 and 1, not an electron count.

options.text: A strong covalent bond or lone pair
options.why: Bonds and lone pairs show values close to 1.

options.text: That the region is vacuum
options.why: Regions with almost no density can give noisy ELF values, but a broad plateau near 0.5 inside a crystal is the uniform-gas signature, not emptiness.

hints: What value does a uniform electron gas give?
Which value marks a localized electron pair?

visual.caption: Face-centred cubic: the structure of many metals.
visual.alt: Face-centred cubic cell: an atom at each corner and in the middle of each face of a cube.

prompt: A CHGCAR grid has 40 x 40 x 40 points, and the sum of all its values is 512000. How many valence electrons are in the cell?
hints: The electron count is the average of the grid values.
